title: Compact completion and uniform statistical bounds for hyperbolic geodesic sliced Wasserstein distance
shortTitle: Hyperbolic sliced Wasserstein: what it really measures
oneLine: Geodesic sliced Wasserstein distance on hyperbolic space is exactly a weak-convergence metric on the compact closed Klein ball: it has an exact diameter, barely sees depth far from the centre, gives squared distance π·α between boundary points at angle α in two dimensions, and can be estimated at optimal rates with no assumptions on the data.
abstract: Data such as trees, hierarchies and networks are often embedded in hyperbolic space, and geodesic hyperbolic sliced Wasserstein distance (Bonet et al., 2023) compares two such data clouds cheaply by projecting them onto geodesics through a fixed centre and averaging one-dimensional transport costs. This candidate determines exactly what that distance measures. In the Klein ball each projection is atanh(v·z), and its angular moments stay uniformly bounded even at the ideal boundary. Hence, for every dimension d ≥ 2 and 1 ≤ p < ∞, the distance extends with no moment assumption to all probability measures; its completion is the space of probability measures on the compact closed Klein ball, it metrises weak convergence there, and its diameter is exactly 2C_{d,p}^{1/p}. Mass escaping to infinity converges to the boundary sphere instead of disappearing, so the distance cannot control hyperbolic transport moments and is exponentially insensitive to depth far from the centre, with exact radial rates. The induced metric on the boundary sphere is found in every dimension: squared distance π·α in two dimensions, (1/2)α² log(1/α) behaviour in three, and comparable to α² from four on. An explicit function shows that the vanishing-at-infinity assertion of Proposition 19 in Bonet, Drumetz and Courty (JMLR 2025) fails. Sampling error obeys distribution-free n^(-1/2) bounds for the powered loss, in expectation and with high probability, at minimax-optimal rates; adding one radial Wasserstein term gives a complete metric with the usual hyperbolic Wasserstein topology. The separation mechanism is credited to Lyons (2014). AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

Two scripts give floating-point sanity checks: 36 projection instances against direct minimisation, six quadratic angular constants against trigamma values, 12 backprojection evaluations, seven dilogarithm/boundary comparisons, 24 radial cases over eight (d,p) pairs, ten exact binomial sums, Legendre coefficients, the d = 3 series against quadrature, the d ≥ 4 small-angle constant and a near-critical radial constant. Both scripts were replayed with and without Python -O from fresh copies with byte-identical outputs; a corrupted boundary identity is rejected under -O; GitHub CI reruns both on Linux. keyResults: Compact completion (Theorem 2.3): for d ≥ 2 and 1 ≤ p < ∞, geodesic hyperbolic sliced Wasserstein distance extends with no moment assumption; its completion is the space of probability measures on the compact closed Klein ball, it metrises weak convergence there, and its diameter is exactly 2C_{d,p}^{1/p} (π in the plane for p = 2).

Correction (Proposition 3.1): for g(t,v) = sech²t the geodesic backprojection equals 1 − tanh²r/d, which tends to 1 − 1/d at infinity, so the C₀ claim of Proposition 19 in Bonet, Drumetz and Courty (JMLR 2025) fails.

Depth insensitivity (Theorem 4.1, Corollary 4.2): the squared distance between a point at depth r and its boundary point decays like e^{−(d−1)r}, r e^{−2pr} or e^{−2pr} according as d − 1 is below, equal to or above 2p; far-out points on one ray are exponentially close however far apart they are.

Boundary geometry (Proposition 4.3, Theorem 4.4): for p = 2 the squared distance between boundary points at angle α is exactly πα when d = 2, behaves like (1/2)α² log(1/α) when d = 3, and is comparable to α² with limit constant (d−2)/((d−1)(d−3)) when d ≥ 4.

Estimation and repair (Theorems 5.1, 5.2, Corollary 5.3, Theorem 6.1): distribution-free sampling error n^{−1/2} for the powered loss in expectation and with high probability, minimax-optimal rates n^{−1/2} and n^{−1/(2p)}; adding one radial Wasserstein term gives a complete metric with the usual hyperbolic Wasserstein topology.

narration: What does a popular distance for hyperbolic data really measure? An Evidence Press briefing. Data such as family trees, word hierarchies and social networks are often placed in hyperbolic space, a geometry in which room grows very quickly as you move away from the centre. To compare two clouds of such points, machine-learning methods use a sliced Wasserstein distance: project both clouds onto many lines through a fixed centre, compare them along each line and average the results. This candidate paper works out exactly what that average detects. The projections stay bounded on average, even at infinity. So the distance extends to the closed ball, boundary sphere included, and mass that drifts off to infinity simply lands on that boundary. The distance has an exact maximum, detects ordinary weak convergence, and barely sees depth: two points far out in the same direction look almost the same, however far apart they really are. In two dimensions, the squared distance between two points at infinity is exactly pi times the angle between them, and the paper gives the boundary geometry in every dimension. It also corrects a published claim, Proposition nineteen of Bonet, Drumetz and Courty, proves that the distance can be estimated from samples at the best possible rate with no assumptions on the data, and shows that adding one comparison of distances from the centre restores the usual hyperbolic notion of convergence. The proofs are written out; the numerical checks are only sanity checks. The results cover the exact average over all directions from a fixed centre. This is an unrefereed candidate with internal AI-assisted review only. Released on the fourth of November 2026; the paper, code and data are linked from the release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional evidence.
